title: Preparedness for the AI Era Requires a Reserve of Critical Workers
gist: RAND's Carter C. Price argues that because AI job-displacement timing is highly uncertain, governments should build a funded 'reserve force' of critical workers (training slots, retention incentives, documentation, drills) so essential services survive if AI fails, is hacked, or arrives late; markets won't fund this redundancy on their own.

insights.claim: Forecasts about which jobs AI will eliminate and when are typically made with far more confidence than the evidence supports, and claims of imminent AI-driven mass unemployment appear premature.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Discount aggressive near-term AI-labor-displacement narratives; timing risk cuts both ways for AI-adoption trades.
insights.quote: forecasts about exactly what kind of jobs will disappear and when are often made with far more confidence than evidence warrants

insights.claim: Geoff Hinton's 2016 advice to stop training radiologists because AI would soon replace them looks premature a decade later.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: A canonical failed AI-replacement prediction; useful base rate for skepticism on specific occupation displacement timelines.
insights.quote: A decade later, his advice looks premature.

insights.claim: Uncertainty about AI timing discourages prospective workers from spending years and thousands of dollars on training for careers that may not be stable.

insights.claim: If governments or employers assume permanent automation is imminent, vital training and career pipelines could collapse, leaving society short of people for essential work.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Premature pipeline cuts can create acute shortages in essential skills—a second-order risk of AI hype.

insights.claim: COBOL, though still critical to many government systems, has been treated as obsolete for decades, so its training pipeline effectively shut off and the number of programmers who know it dwindled.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Legacy-system skill scarcity is a recurring operational risk for governments and incumbents; modernization vendors benefit.

insights.claim: When 24 million workers lost jobs at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, states had to call COBOL programmers out of retirement to keep unemployment benefits systems running.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Crisis-driven demand spikes expose brittle public IT; shows the cost of letting skill pipelines lapse.

insights.claim: Policymakers should not try to predict the labor market precisely but should choose policies that leave the population less exposed if AI projections turn out wrong.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price

insights.claim: RAND's Price proposes a 'reserve force of critical workers' in public and private sectors, consisting of funded training slots, retention incentives for experienced workers, formal procedure documentation, and a reserve pool that is periodically recertified and drilled.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Potential new public spending stream for training providers, workforce-development and documentation/knowledge-management vendors.
insights.quote: funded training slots, retention incentives for experienced workers, formal documentation of procedures, and a reserve pool that receives periodic recertification and participates in drills

insights.claim: A human workforce reserve would keep vital services running if AI systems are hacked, shut down, or less reliable than promised, functioning like backup generators or strategic stockpiles.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Frames AI-failure/cyber risk as a resilience problem; supports demand for human-in-the-loop fallback and cyber resilience spending.
insights.quote: Like backup generators and strategic stockpiles, a reserve force of critical workers may look unproductive—until the day it is needed.

insights.claim: Markets are good at cutting costs but poor at preserving surplus capacity for emergencies, so building resilience against AI failure requires government coordination.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Expect regulatory mandates for redundancy in critical sectors that may cap labor-cost savings from AI automation.

themes.theme: Implementation via CISA's critical functions and pilots

insights.claim: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has already identified 55 National Critical Functions, each dependent on specific human roles such as grid dispatchers, water-treatment operators, and emergency clinicians, which can define what counts as 'critical'.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: The 55 NCFs offer a ready-made map of which occupations and operators could face workforce-preservation mandates.

insights.claim: Preserving critical human capacity involves maintaining detailed documentation, resourcing existing training pipelines, building human-led fallback procedures for every automated critical system, and drilling enough people to run manual backups, akin to the National Guard's peacetime readiness model.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: Automating critical systems may carry added compliance costs for manual fallback and drills.
insights.quote: Develop human-led fallback procedures for any critical system that is automated.

insights.claim: State and local policymakers could begin with pilot programs that document critical functions, map critical-task processes and identify critical skills, then scale successful pilots to other sectors.
insights.speaker: Carter C. Price
insights.so_what: State-level pilots are the likely first venue for AI-resilience workforce policy; watch for early adopters.

insights.claim: Long-term public commitments to preserve human roles in critical sectors would reduce uncertainty for students and early-career workers and keep those fields viable careers regardless of AI outcomes.
